rules.title: Security deposit cap of 1.5 months' rent (Security Deposit Law)
rules.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit greater than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rent, including last month's rent, counts toward the cap, so no more than 2.5 months' rent may be required at lease inception.
rules.key_value: 1.5x monthly rent; annual deposit increase max 10%
rules.quoted_span: The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ).
rules.coverage_text: The Security Deposit Law applies to most residential rental properties, including mobile homes.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings, unless the tenant opts in by written request (applies 30 days after the request).
rules.extraction_note: Source is a DCA informational guide summarizing state law. No penalty stated specifically for exceeding the cap; the guide states double damages plus costs and attorney's fees for wrongful withholding at return (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1). No effective or enactment date given.

rules.title: Anti-Eviction Act good cause requirement
rules.requirement: A residential landlord may not evict a tenant or refuse to renew a written or oral lease without one of the statutory good causes, such as nonpayment, disorderly conduct, damage, rule or lease violations, or an unpaid lawful rent increase. A Notice to Quit, and for some causes a Notice to Cease, is required, with notice periods from three days to three years depending on the cause.
rules.key_value: Good cause required for eviction and non-renewal
rules.quoted_span: No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.
rules.coverage_text: The Anti-Eviction Act applies to most residential rental properties including single-family homes, mobile homes and land in a mobile home park, apartment buildings, and complexes, and rooming and boarding homes.
rules.exemptions: May not apply to two- or three-unit owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units; hotel, motel or guest house transient or seasonal guests (unless the occupant has no alternate residence and lives there continually); units held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member who permanently occupies the unit.
rules.penalty: Landlord who evicts for owner occupancy and does not occupy the unit for 6 months, or who returns a board-up, demolition or retirement property to residential use within 5 years, is liable for three times damages plus attorney fees and costs; civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation for the retirement/removal case (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.6).
rules.extraction_note: Source is a DCA informational guide. Owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings follow a separate eviction procedure under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2(a). No effective or enactment date given.

rules.title: Relocation assistance for illegal-occupancy evictions
rules.requirement: A tenant evicted so the landlord can correct an illegal occupancy is entitled to relocation assistance from the landlord equal to six times the monthly rent. If the landlord does not pay at least five days before removal, the tenant may be paid from a municipal revolving fund, which the landlord must repay.
rules.quoted_span: Any tenant evicted under G 3) (illegal occupancy) is entitled to relocation assistance in an amount equal to six times the tenant’s monthly rent.
rules.coverage_text: Tenants evicted under cause G 3) (correction of illegal occupancy).
rules.penalty: If no municipal relocation fund exists and the landlord pays late, interest accrues at 18% per year until paid; the amount due is a lien on the property.
rules.extraction_note: Guide also states a Notice to Quit at least three months before filing is required for cause G evictions and that relocation assistance must be provided before eviction. The guide cites alternative statutory subsections.

rules.title: Rent increases must not be unconscionable
rules.requirement: New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but a rent increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. The landlord must terminate the existing lease with proper notice and offer a new lease at the higher rent; the rent cannot be raised mid-lease.
rules.quoted_span: The increase in rent must not be unconscionable; it must not be so unreasonable as to shock the conscience of a fair and honest person and must comply with any municipal ordinances governing rent increases.
rules.coverage_text: Residential tenancies covered by the Anti-Eviction Act; municipalities may separately adopt rent control or rent leveling ordinances.
rules.exemptions: Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control ordinances for 30 years after completion (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). HUD-owned or subsidized housing and NJHMFA-controlled projects are not subject to municipal rent control.
rules.interaction: Municipal rent control ordinances, where adopted, also govern rent increases. A tenant may complain to the municipal rent control board where one exists; otherwise a court decides unconscionability in an eviction action.
rules.extraction_note: Unconscionability factors (per case law): size of increase, landlord's expenses and profitability, comparable rents, bargaining position, and the judge's general knowledge. A tenant may withhold the disputed increase but risks an eviction suit.

rules.title: No rent increases to cover conversion costs
rules.requirement: When a building is converted to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, rents may not be raised to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. Increases for new services or amenities are still allowed.
rules.quoted_span: If a building is converted to a condominium or cooperative form of ownership, or to fee simple ownership of units, rents may not be increased to cover cos ts resulting solely from the conversion (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.31).
rules.coverage_text: All tenants in the converted building, whether or not eligible for protected tenancy.
rules.extraction_note: Quoted span keeps the document's spacing artifact 'cos ts'.

rules.title: Credit report cost and reasonable application fees allowed
rules.requirement: A landlord may charge an applicant for the cost of a credit report and may request reasonable rental application fees. If an application is denied because of a credit report, the landlord must give the name, address and phone number of the reporting agency.
rules.key_value: Cost of report; reasonable application fee
rules.quoted_span: The landlord is allowed to charge the tenant for the cost of the report. The landlord may also request reasonable rental application fees or employment verification.
rules.coverage_text: Prospective tenants screened via credit reports or tenant screening agencies.
rules.extraction_note: The guide states no specific statutory cite for the fee allowance; the cited federal FCRA section concerns adverse-action disclosure. No numeric fee cap is given.

rules.title: Law Against Discrimination: source of lawful income
rules.requirement: Landlords may not refuse to rent to or discriminate against applicants based on protected characteristics, including source of lawful income. The prohibition does not apply to two-family owner-occupied dwellings or rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home.
rules.quoted_span: The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD), N.J.S.A. 10:5-12(g) to -(h), prohibits discrimination when selling or renting property and requires equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender  identity or expression, mental and physical disability, nationality, or source of lawful income.
rules.coverage_text: All landlord-tenant relationships, with listed exceptions.
rules.exemptions: Two-family owner-occupied dwellings; rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home; single-sex residences (e.g., YMCA) and age-restricted housing as to familial status (N.J.S.A. 10:5-5(n)).
rules.penalty: Monetary damages, an order to rent the unit to the complainant, and fines and penalties up to $10,000 for a first offense (N.J.S.A. 10:5-14.1a(a)).
rules.extraction_note: The document does not address criminal-history screening limits. Quoted span preserves the document's double space in 'gender  identity'.
